newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel welcomes Bonn parliament backing for accord.
newsitem.headline: Havel welcomes Bonn parliament backing for accord.

text.p: President Vaclav Havel welcomed on Thursday the Bonn parliament's overwhelming backing for a Czech-German reconciliation accord and said he believed the Czech parliament would also approve it.
The German parliament approved the declaration, which is intended to banish any lingering resentments from World War Two and its aftermath, by 578 votes to 20 with 23 abstentions.

"The president of the republic welcomes the approval of the Czech-German declaration in the (German) Federal assembly and is pleased that the resolution was carried by a large majority," a statement from Havel's press secretary, Ladislav Spacek, said.

The declaration was signed by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus in Prague last week. In the accord, Bonn expresses sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague its regret for the post-war expulsion of 2.5 million ethnic Germans.
The accord does not need formal ratification but the Czech parliament is also scheduled to vote on it next month.
"The president firmly believes that the declaration will be accepted by both houses of parliament of the Czech Republic," the statement form Havel's office said.
"Above all acceptance of the declaration itself is at stake, the president considers it to be an important step in building good relations among European nations," it added.
The declaration also includes German support for Czech membership of the European Union.
However, it remains highly controversial in both countries.
Czech parliament chairman Milos Zeman, in Bonn, asked Germany's parliamentary parties on Tuesday for a last-minute rider to the accord.
Zeman's Social Democrats (CSSD), the largest Czech opposition party, have reservations about the text of the accord, hammered out during two years of tortuous negotiations.
"The president considers the acceptance of any accompanying resolution as secondary," the statement said.
